articles.title: Europe, US closer than they look on tech rules, says EU tech chief
articles.description: “The same companies, the same practices, are under investigation and under discussion.”
articles.summary: “The same companies, the same practices, are under investigation and under discussion.”
articles.content:
EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen on Wednesday played down the regulatory gulf between Brussels and Washington, arguing that US courts end up policing the same companies for the same behavior that European law targets in advance.

“The differences are not so big when we look at it in practice,” the European Commission’s executive vice-president for tech sovereignty told AFP on the sidelines of a G20 meeting of technology ministers in North Carolina.

“In Europe, we have regulation in advance, and in the USA they are often coming with the court cases,” she said. “The same companies, the same practices, are under investigation and under discussion.”

Her remarks came after two days of sessions in which the ministers were addressed by industry figures including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Elon Musk, who used the platform to repeat the familiar charge that Europe over-regulates technology.

Virkkunen said she did not accept the premise.

“We don’t see, and I don’t see, that innovation and regulation are opposite things,” the Finnish official said.

She pointed to a recent Eurobarometer survey published in which 80 percent of European respondents said careful regulation of AI was important for safety reasons.

“For Europeans, it’s important that we can trust these technologies,” she said, while acknowledging that Brussels would bring forward proposals to streamline some EU rules.

She noted that the absence of national tech laws in the United States has not left the industry free of government rules there.

“At (the) state level, there are hundreds of rules now on AI (in the US),” she said. “That is the situation we wanted to avoid with our AI Act — that we have one rule for the whole market.”

Virkkunen said the convergence between Europe and the United States could be seen most clearly in attitudes toward protecting minors on social media.

Meta last month reached a landmark settlement with nearly every US state, promising curfews and time limits for teens on Instagram and Facebook.

Asked about the settlement, she said some of its provisions were already law in Europe under the Digital Services Act, which requires platforms to let users flag illegal content and choose the recommender system that serves them.

But she said Brussels was pursuing the same underlying concerns about how addictive the platforms can be,  an issue that has seen Meta, YouTube and TikTok face thousands of lawsuits in the United States.

The Commission published preliminary findings in July on the addictive design of Meta’s services, and earlier in the summer on how the company checks whether a user is at least 13 years old.

It has also issued preliminary findings against TikTok on addictive design and opened an investigation into Snapchat in the spring.

“We are ready to come up with stronger rules also in Europe on this matter, but I think social media platforms could also do much more now already,” Virkkunen said.

On AI safety, she said the enforcement powers attached to the EU’s AI Act took effect in August, and that most leading AI developers had been cooperating with the Commission voluntarily before then.

“They understand that if they want to operate in the European markets, we have our rules and they have to comply with our rules,” she said.

Asked whether Europe was seeing the kind of local opposition to data centers now spreading in the United States, Virkkunen said the debate was already lively in some EU member states, an outcome she said careful planning was meant to avoid.

She described an imbalance within the bloc, with data center builders gravitating toward countries with abundant cheap clean power.

articles.title: US judge rejects bid to break up Google’s ad business
articles.description: She gave the two sides 30 days to submit a joint proposed final judgment.
articles.summary: She gave the two sides 30 days to submit a joint proposed final judgment.
articles.content:
A US federal judge on Wednesday refused to force Google to sell a division of its digital advertising business, rejecting the government’s push to break up part of the company’s ad empire.

In a court order, US District Court Judge Leonie Brinkema opted instead for a set of rules governing how Google must operate in the ad market.

The decision is the second time in recent years that a federal judge has declined to dismantle a piece of Google’s business, after a judge last year refused to force the sale of its Chrome browser in a separate monopoly case over online search.

Those cases are part of a broader effort by the Department of Justice (DOJ) to curtail the competitive dominance of big tech companies, including Apple, Amazon and Meta. 

Results have been mixed, with another judge deciding against government lawyers in a suit concerning Meta’s social media empire but other decision going the government’s way.

“We’re very pleased the Court rejected the DOJ’s proposal to break apart tools that help small businesses reach new customers and grow,” Google’s vice president of regulatory affairs Lee-Anne Mulholland said in a statement.

The reasoning behind today’s decision was not immediately made public. 

Brinkema filed her opinion under seal for 14 days, leaving the details of how Google must change its ad business unknown for now. 

She gave the two sides 30 days to submit a joint proposed final judgment.

The case focused on Google’s ad tech “stack” — the suite of tools that website publishers use to sell ads and advertisers use to buy them.

Brinkema — whose court is in Alexandria, Virginia outside Washington — ruled last year that Google had willfully monopolized both the publisher ad server and ad exchange markets, and had unlawfully tied the two products together.

Google has said it will appeal the underlying liability ruling.

The government’s case portrayed Google as simultaneously controlling multiple sides of the digital advertising marketplace, owning the platform that publishers use to sell ads as well as the exchange where transactions occur, all while commanding huge advertiser demand. 

According to the Department of Justice, Google once compared this arrangement to Goldman Sachs owning the New York Stock Exchange.

Prosecutors had sought the sale of Google’s ad auction site AdX and the open-sourcing of critical auction technology.

Google characterized the proposed remedies as extreme government overreach that would harm publishers, advertisers and consumers.

It had also argued that splitting up the service would be technically unfeasible.

At closing arguments last year, Brinkema questioned how long a forced sale would take and noted that no buyer for AdX had been identified.

articles.title: Data center backlash scrambles US midterm politics
articles.description: The midwestern former manufacturing hub of Ohio offers perhaps the sharpest test of the politics of data centers.
articles.summary: The midwestern former manufacturing hub of Ohio offers perhaps the sharpest test of the politics of data centers.
articles.content:
The data centers powering America’s artificial intelligence boom have become an unlikely target in November’s midterm elections, as anger over rising electricity bills and noise turns Democrats — and a growing number of Republicans — against Big Tech. 

Candidates in at least 21 races across 18 states have aired television advertisements mentioning data centers this cycle, according to marketing data cited by US media, almost evenly divided between both parties. 

On the grid serving Senate battleground Ohio, as well as 12 other states, demand from data centers drove up capacity costs by $9.3 billion in a single year, a 174 percent increase, according to an independent market monitor. 

Anger over household bills has merged with a broader populist distrust of Silicon Valley, exposing lawmakers who, until recently, were courting the sprawling server farms with tax breaks and promises of jobs and investment. 

In Texas, Republican Governor Greg Abbott has frozen new projects while regulators weigh their impact on power and water supplies. It was Abbott who, not long ago, called his state the “epicenter of AI development.” 

His Democratic challenger wants a moratorium until lawmakers pass stronger safeguards, and accuses Abbott of putting wealthy interests ahead of ordinary Texans. 

In Brazoria — between Houston and the Gulf Coast — 44-year-old Melissa Burnett told AFP the serenity of her quiet neighborhood had been shattered by a 17-megawatt center last year that is “like a freight train always coming at you.” 

“We were not supposed to hear it, nor was it supposed to affect our quality of life, and it’s just done the opposite, you know?” she said.

Almost alone among Republicans, President Donald Trump has not moved. He still calls the industry essential to beating China on AI, leaving him at odds with candidates running under his own banner. 

– ‘Sleeper issue’ –

The midwestern former manufacturing hub of Ohio offers perhaps the sharpest test of the politics of data centers. 

Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who lost his Senate berth in 2024, is running for the Buckeye State’s other seat. Brown has run at least four ads attacking Republican Jon Husted for courting data center investment as lieutenant governor. 

They brand Husted “the face of data centers,” and Brown has promised to make operators pay the full cost of the power they use. 

Senate Republicans have warned that the issue could cost Husted the race. Their campaign arm called data centers a “sleeper issue” and said a defeat blamed on them would chill political support for the industry nationwide. 

The same argument is turning up in races that have little else in common: a Republican running for governor in Florida promising to shield families from facilities that push up utility bills; a Pennsylvania Democrat demanding that tech companies cover their own costs; a Wyoming Republican who won a House primary on advertisements attacking Silicon Valley billionaires. 

In Michigan, the issue toppled two better-connected Democrats in a primary won by a leftist who said opposition had united committed Republicans, Trump voters, independents and Democrats. 

– Both parties turn –

In Wisconsin, Republican gubernatorial nominee Tom Tiffany has taken to calling his Democratic opponent “Data Center David Crowley.” Earlier this year Tiffany was praising the technology and voting to speed AI infrastructure through. 

Tiffany now wants the state’s tax incentives scrapped and the industry more tightly regulated, though he stops short of a ban. 

Democratic governors are moving the same way. 

New York has imposed a year-long moratorium on new hyperscale facilities, and Pennsylvania now requires developers to cover infrastructure costs and meet tougher standards on water use, hiring and community consultation. 

Trump has not moved with them. 

“America must remain dominant in the AI race that is the future. I think the American people understand that, and this president certainly does,” his spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt said on Thursday.

His administration has signed up Google, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, xAI, OpenAI and Amazon to a voluntary “Ratepayer Protection Pledge.” 

Under it, the companies undertake not to leave consumers paying for the power plants and grid upgrades their facilities require.

articles.title: ‘Imposing ignorance’: US climate science under siege
articles.description: The Arctic is warming several times faster than the global average, a phenomenon known as “Arctic ampl
articles.summary: The Arctic is warming several times faster than the global average, a phenomenon known as “Arctic ampl
articles.content:
A benchmark US report on the fast-changing state of the Arctic has been canceled. The nation’s top research body has removed a chapter on global warming from a reference manual for judges.

After the mass layoffs and budget cuts of the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term, the administration is barreling ahead in its war on climate science, at a time when the world’s oceans and land masses face record-breaking heat.

In 2025, the Arctic Report Card, cancelled this week, found the polar region had experienced its hottest year since records began, with cascading impacts from melting glaciers and sea ice to greening landscapes and disruptions to global weather.

“The Arctic is a bellwether of climate change,” Rick Spinrad, a former administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), told AFP. “They’re imposing ignorance on the system in the hopes that that will address the challenges that are real associated with climate change.”

– Global impacts –

The Arctic is warming several times faster than the global average, a phenomenon known as “Arctic amplification” — and the effects aren’t confined to the North Pole.

For example, losing sea ice injects more freshwater into the North Atlantic, making surface waters less dense and salty and hindering their ability to sink and drive the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which helps keep Europe’s winters milder.

NOAA, which has published the Report Card annually since 2006, did not explain its demise, saying only that “Coordination of the 2026 Arctic Report Card will not be facilitated through NOAA” and that prior data would remain publicly available.

It is the latest in a long line of actions by the Trump administration against science documenting the impacts of human-caused climate change.

Last week, the National Academy of Sciences, a Congressionally-chartered yet independent body, removed from its website a chapter on climate science from a manual for judges.

It came after Trump took to Truth Social to blast the chapter as “fraudulent, biased and misleading” and accuse the NAS of being run by “Radical Left Democrats.”

A statement by the NAS alluded to “considerable scrutiny,” adding it had determined “that questions about the processes used to develop the chapter warrant an independent review, and the chapter will not appear on our website while that review is underway.” 

A spokesperson told AFP on Wednesday: “We expect to complete the review this fall.”

The decision attracted attention particularly because the NAS had weeks earlier released a comprehensive review of climate attribution science.

That review examined whether individual extreme weather events can be linked to climate change and found the science robust for many phenomena — a question pivotal to dozens of cases against oil and gas companies working their way through US courts.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Canada and the world vs the hidden risks of tech infrastructure and supply chains
articles.description: AI has also rewritten the playbook. Used properly, AI can drastically reduce operational costs for suppliers and businesses through sheer efficiency.
articles.summary: AI has also rewritten the playbook. Used properly, AI can drastically reduce operational costs for suppliers and businesses through sheer efficiency.
articles.content:
The more garish aspects of new tech are easy enough to see and almost impossible to avoid. Trade realities are infuriating but obvious. Far less obvious and likely to be the bedrock issues for global tech are technological supply chains and infrastructure dependence.

In a commendably clear article, Ms Nancy Wilson CPA spells out the Canadian situation for small businesses on Rabble.ca. She points out that Canada’s heirloom relationship with the US created an automatic dependency for Canadian small businesses which is now a problem.

Citing infrastructure and front- and back-end supply issues, from shopfronts to platforms and costs, she explains that a vast number of core business operations flow through this environment.

Everything from hosting to cloud storage, accounts operations, e-commerce, payment systems, and other fundamentals are entangled in the old US relationships and resulting current cluster. Wilson also gives an example of the broader issues, like the Canadian Loonie getting poleaxed in relation to the US dollar as another reality bite.

The necessary evolution of infrastructure and trade

The major issue is that Canada and the world are now having to dig their way out of the general mess. This is necessary to achieve any level of sovereignty and mobility within the infrastructure.

AI has also rewritten the playbook. Used properly, AI can drastically reduce operational costs for suppliers and businesses through sheer efficiency. These are AI’s strong suits.

Forget agents, chatbots, and other ornaments. They’re third wheels, interfaces, and in most cases just higher data load capacity respectively. The real value of AI is likely to come in do-everything packages, like China’s instant software and support business models.

These are the likely outcomes for sustainable business, and they must be competitive in their markets. Just sign up and you’re ready to go.  International trade is global whether anyone likes it or not. This is globalization the reality, as opposed to globalization the easy target for illiterates.

That doesn’t solve the risk factors, though. A data-centre-dependent environment could generate a lot of outages. It could create monopolies where cost is “at will”, not based on competitive principles. It’s an evolved and much more complex version of the same issues Wilson describes, magnified exponentially.

Supply chain issues, trade relationships, and solutions

The supply chains underpin trade and the conduct of daily business from the top to the bottom. These supply chains are almost invisible in daily life. Every transaction, every social media post, every online ad, and every move is dependent on these supply chains working properly.

As AI moves in, which it must, the sheer clunkiness of current AI is likely to be a risk to critical supply chains. Who actually needs billions of unpredictable AI agents for daily personal business?  

They’re a novelty, not a necessity, unless you actually are that lazy and hands-off on your own business. The platforms will be AI anyway. Why add layers and costs of unnecessary, unreliable AI operations to basic business operations?

This is the rationale that is likely to reinvent supply chains. “Get rid of the middlemen” applies just as forcefully to AI as it does to third parties in transactions. Data centre modernization is already a default search term as AI catches up with its new iterations and updates current infrastructure simply to manage energy realities and new technologies.

Supply chains have to respond to demand. Business will dictate the infrastructure as demands diversify far beyond current technologies and their current issues.

The trade and sovereignty issues sing from the same hymn book. Adam Smith pointed out in The Wealth of Nations that trade is about doing real business and making money, not supporting old trade models.

Canadian trade issues are a good agar plate for defining the fixes. If nations take a hands-on approach to ensuring their own local supply chains, things have to change for the better.

articles.title: Elevate Festival brings Canadian tech closer to customers and capital
articles.description: Twelve months later, many of the same pressures are still on the minds of Canadian innovators
articles.summary: Twelve months later, many of the same pressures are still on the minds of Canadian innovators
articles.content:
A year ago, Lisa Zarzeczny described a Canadian innovation ecosystem at a crossroads.

“We are at a really pivotal moment here in Canada, and the stakes are high for all Canadians,” said the cofounder and CEO of non-profit innovation organization Elevate when we spoke in 2025, alluding to the country’s relationship with the U.S. that had already started to buckle, the rise of AI, and the digital sovereignty questions at the heart of both. 

Twelve months later, many of the same pressures are still on the minds of Canadian innovators.

Access to capital, finding customers, and the challenge of helping Canadian companies grow here while competing globally are all still on the table. 

“The stakes only continue to get higher,” Zarzeczny says in a statement. “Which is why conversations around AI and sovereignty are at the forefront of this year’s programming. Canada already has the talent and the ambition. Our job is to turn that potential into momentum.” 

The festival returns to Toronto Sept. 22-24 for its ninth year, with roughly 10,000 attendees expected at Meridian Hall and the St. Lawrence Centre. 

This year brings a new sovereign growth content track, exploring how Canada can create a stronger innovation economy while competing on a global scale. It also includes more opportunities for founder-investor meetings, new hands-on crash courses about essential tools, and a new AI-powered networking app designed to help people find the right person in a very large room.

Customers are part of the scale-up problem

Ahead of this year’s event, Zarzeczny and I sat down again to look at how things have changed, and what needs to happen so homegrown companies can stay here while competing on a global scale.

She admits it’s not an easy answer, and kept coming back to two things Canadian startups need.

Capital and customers.

“Canadian companies have had to go abroad to find their first customers,” she says. “So from both corporate Canada and the public service, becoming adopters of Canadian solutions is such a huge piece of that. We’ve noticed the rhetoric change there, so now I’d like to see activity and action change there as well.”

An August study from the Council of Canadian Innovators identified access to customers as one of four structural barriers companies hit as they scale. 

Founders told researchers that early domestic customers can be difficult to secure, with buyers wanting evidence of global customers first.

Zarzeczny hears the same frustration from founders.

When they approach customers outside Canada, she says, one of the first questions is which Canadian companies are they working with?

“We need to be that proof-point for startups and become their first customers, and then have them scale globally,” she says.

articles.title: The brand doom loop: Why companies are rethinking marketing in the age of AI
articles.description: One of the challenges associated with branding is that failure is rarely immediate.
articles.summary: One of the challenges associated with branding is that failure is rarely immediate.
articles.content:
Most business leaders worry about disruptive competitors, changing customer expectations, or new technologies. Fewer worry about something more subtle: brand drift. Yet according to recent research from Gartner, 84% of companies are trapped in what analysts describe as a “brand doom loop,” a cycle in which organizations underinvest in brand measurement, lose confidence in brand performance, and subsequently reduce investment even further. The result is a gradual erosion of brand relevance that can directly affect growth.

The findings arrive at a particularly important time. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how customers discover, evaluate, and engage with businesses. As search engines increasingly incorporate AI-generated responses and recommendation systems become more influential, companies are being forced to reconsider whether their brands are equipped for a rapidly changing digital marketplace.

According to Gartner, organizations caught in the brand doom loop are only half as likely to exceed growth targets compared with companies that successfully evaluate and manage brand performance. The firm also predicts that by 2028, more than 80% of companies will make significant changes to their identity, mission, culture, or brand in response to AI-driven market changes.

When brands stop working

One of the challenges associated with branding is that failure is rarely immediate. Instead, things tend to dissipate over time. For instance, a product defect is usually obvious. Instead, a sales collapse is visible in quarterly results. Brand deterioration tends to happen gradually. A company may continue operating successfully for years while its market position steadily weakens. Messaging that once resonated with customers becomes dated. Competitors reposition themselves. Customer priorities evolve. New technologies alter buying behaviour.

Nothing appears broken, but performance begins to decline. This phenomenon is drawing increasing attention from brand strategists such as Karen Tiber Leland, president of Sterling Marketing Group and author of the forthcoming book Re-Up Your Brand. Leland argues that many organizations respond incorrectly when they notice declining brand performance.

Instead of conducting expensive and disruptive rebranding exercises, she advocates a more continuous process of reassessment and adjustment. The distinction reflects an important shift in thinking. Traditional rebranding often treats branding as a project that is completed and then left unchanged for years. A “re-up” approach assumes that brands require regular maintenance and adaptation to remain relevant.

articles.title: Dutch shift 86 tonnes of gold from US, Canada to UK
articles.description: “This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” said the bank in a statement.
articles.summary: “This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” said the bank in a statement.
articles.content:
The Dutch central bank said Wednesday it had moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the United States and Canada to London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest.”

The DNB bank said gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily than those held in New York and Ottawa.

“This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” said the bank in a statement.

“With this step, we have improved the deployability of the gold reserves. We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” said DNB President Olaf Sleijpen.

The total Dutch gold stock amounted to 612.4 tonnes and was valued at 72.2 billion euros at the end of 2025, said the DNB.

Before the deployment, the Dutch bank held 31.3 percent of its gold in New York and 19.7 percent in Ottawa. 

After the move, each country accounted for 18.5 percent of the Dutch gold reserve.

The share of gold held in London increased from 18.1 percent to 32.1 percent. The bank still holds 30.8 percent of its gold in the Netherlands.

The transfer was carried out partially by buying and selling and partly by physically transferring gold, said the bank.

The bank moved more than 27 tonnes of physical gold from the United States and Canada to Zeist.

The same quantity of gold was moved from Zeist to London, preventing the melting down of gold bars.

“By combining buying and selling and physical transport, the risks associated with physically moving a large quantity of gold have been spread,” said the DNB.

The operation took place between March and August of this year, the bank said.

– ‘Deepest and most liquid’ –

Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based National Gold Counter, which facilitates gold trading in France, said central banks had been moving their reserves around for about a decade.

“The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations,” Schwartz told AFP.

The London market is the deepest and most liquid, said Schwartz, making it easier to deploy in times of crisis.

“Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions,” he added. 

John Plassard, analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, told AFP the Dutch move was intended “for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis.”

For the moment, it was a “fairly one-off move” but he warned that if other central banks followed suit, it could damage confidence in the United States.

At the beginning of the year, there were concerns raised in Germany about the security of their central bank’s reserves in New York.

However, the powerful Bundesbank has decided for the moment not to shift its reserves away from New York.

“The New York Fed is and remains an important storage site for our gold,” the bank told public TV station ARD in January.

articles.title: Stocks drop as Warsh fans US rate hike bets, crude up on US-Iran strikes
articles.description: Warsh said: “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving.
articles.summary: Warsh said: “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving.
articles.content:
With inflation remaining stubbornly high — largely on the back of elevated energy costs — the US central bank has come under pressure to act, and Warsh’s refusal to provide guidance has stoked uncertainty.

But in a highly anticipated speech at the Jackson Hole symposium of central bankers and economists in Wyoming, he left traders with few doubts that he was ready to increase borrowing costs.

Warsh said: “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.”

He called the spike in inflation — currently at 3.7 percent and nearly double the Fed’s two-percent target — “concerning”, and said he would be “hard-pressed” to describe current financial conditions as “restrictive”, a potential hint that rate hikes could be on the horizon.

However, he stopped short of saying he would support a hike, adding: “I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision.”

All three main indexes on Wall Street fell Friday. Yields on short-term US Treasury bonds — which reflect monetary policy expectations — jumped, and the dollar rallied against its peers. Gold, which benefits from lower interest rates, fell.

And Asia followed suit, with tech firms — which rely on borrowing to fuel their huge AI investments — leading the way down.

Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei and Jakarta were all down, though Singapore and Wellington edged up.

Focus will now turn to a string of crucial data releases over the next two weeks before the Fed makes its decision, with jobs up this week and the consumer price index (CPI) next week.

“Should we get an inline payrolls print that does not give the Fed too much to work with, next week’s core CPI report will become the major decider for the market’s Fed belief system,” wrote Chris Weston at Pepperstone.

“The volatility priced around that outcome across rates, forex and equities could therefore be significant.”

The Fed’s battle against inflation has been hobbled by the Iran war, which has pushed oil prices higher.

And after a run lower for most of last week, they spiked again Monday, a day after the United States said it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on a small island in the Strait of Hormuz, its first strikes on the country in a month.

The attack prompted Tehran to retaliate by hitting US military targets in Jordan. Both main crude contracts rose more than two percent Monday.

The exchange came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.

The news revived concerns about the conflict, with attempts and peace talks appearing to be going nowhere and the strait — through which a fifth of global crude and gas passes — largely closed.

US officials this month vowed the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran to make it open the waterway.

“Hormuz is once again threatening to put a floor under oil just as Warsh is putting a ceiling on how much inflation patience markets should assume from the Fed,” said Quintex Intel’s Stephen Innes.

“For oil traders, (the) move is another reminder of how quickly the geopolitical premium can return.

“Physical flows through Hormuz have improved materially from their worst levels, which is precisely why crude had started giving back some of the fear premium, but the latest exchange shows how fragile that progress remains and how quickly the shipping story can be pushed back onto the trading desk.”

articles.title: Bond yields are surging: Here’s why that could spell trouble
articles.description: Yields on government-issued debt rise when investors demand higher interest rates to buy or hold bonds.
articles.summary: Yields on government-issued debt rise when investors demand higher interest rates to buy or hold bonds.
articles.content:
From Japan to Europe and the United States, officials are getting antsy as bond yields hit highs not seen in a decade or more, making borrowing more expensive for governments as well as businesses and consumers.

The main reason is soaring deficits and the resulting debt piles, which are fuelling doubts among investors that countries will get their financial houses in order.

And stubbornly high inflation in Europe and the US has accelerated further as the Middle East war pushes up energy prices, which may require central banks to raise interest rates.

– Where are rates now? –

Yields on government-issued debt rise when investors demand higher interest rates to buy or hold bonds.

US Treasury bonds have long been considered among the safest investments available, allowing Washington to borrow money from around the world at favourable rates.

But the yield on 30-year Treasuries, a gauge of long-term confidence in the economy, hit 5.34 percent in mid-August, the highest since 2007, before the global financial crisis.

It has since fallen back to around 5.17 percent.

The trend is similar in Europe, where the benchmark 10-year German bund is yielding around 3.22 percent, a level not seen since 2011.

In France, where the government is struggling to make spending cuts ahead of next year’s presidential election, the 10-year OAT stands at 4.05 percent, the highest since 2008 and well above the 3.5-percent yield at the beginning of the year.

Even in Japan, which for years had yields close to zero as the government grappled with deflation, the 10-year yield has jumped to nearly 2.9 percent from just 2.1 percent in February.

– Why are they rising? –

Government spending in several major economies has soared, and investors have little faith that governments will take tough steps to control their budgets.

“Since the major financial crisis of 2008-2009, public debt has kept growing around the world,” said Frederik Ducrozet, head of macroeconomic research at the Swiss bank Pictet.

And “since the Covid pandemic, the start of the Iran war, and the trade wars, we’ve had a series of shocks” that have required massive spending to withstand, he said.

Charlotte de Montpellier, an economist at ING, noted that even “countries that usually know how to tighten their belts, like Germany, are seeing their deficits climb as well”.

And since governments have to issue ever more bonds to finance those deficits, “they are competing among themselves to attract capital”, she said.

That means they have to offer higher interest rates to borrow — with the yields on bonds already on the market effectively telling them how high they will go. 

– What’s the price to pay? –

Governments are also now competing for cash with technology companies that are borrowing massively to fuel the artificial intelligence boom.

The situation is especially alarming in the United States, where government debt topped $40 trillion for the first time this month.

That is double the total debt from just 10 years ago, and servicing costs have ballooned as a result — money that could otherwise be spent on health care or defence or education.

Last year the interest outlays for Washington hit a whopping $970 billion, up from $350 billion in 2021.

All this comes at a time when bond investors are unsure what the new head of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, is going to do about inflation running at 3.7 percent — nearly double the Fed’s two-percent target.

“One of the reasons for this increase in yields… is the uncertainty about US monetary policy,” de Montpellier said.

“Since Warsh’s arrival, he wants to communicate less, he’s been a bit vague,” she said, referring to his reluctance to give guidance on future Fed rate moves.

“But we know that what happens in the US is going to have a very strong impact on bond markets and interest rates in general,” she said.

articles.title: US national debt exceeds $40 trillion for first time
articles.description: The uptick in borrowing comes as longer term US obligations linked to social security and health care have been growing, while interest payments have climbed as well.
articles.summary: The uptick in borrowing comes as longer term US obligations linked to social security and health care have been growing, while interest payments have climbed as well.
articles.content:
The US gross national debt has surged past $40 trillion for the first time, government data showed Wednesday, outstripping earlier forecasts at a pace fuelled in part by President Donald Trump’s invalidated tariffs.

Total public debt outstanding stood at $40.05 trillion at the close of business Tuesday, according to data released Wednesday by the Treasury Department.

This stands in contrast to an earlier forecast by the Congressional Budget Office that overall borrowing would hit $39.4 trillion by the end of fiscal year 2026.

Rising US debt comes as concerns over inflation, war in the Middle East and government spending have been driving investor worries, and the cost of borrowing has grown.

Yields on long-term Treasury bonds rose Tuesday to the highest level since 2007, reflecting growing price pressures due to war on Iran and anxiety over US deficit spending.

The increase forces the US government to refinance debt at the highest rates since before the 2008 global financial crisis.

But the US Treasury Department moved to steady the long-term bond market early Wednesday, sending yields lower.

The federal government operates at a deficit and borrows money to help cover its obligations, including its war spending and tax cuts.

“It’s been well known for a while that the United States government was on a pretty unsustainable path with deficits,” said Jessica Riedl, a budget and tax fellow at the Brookings Institution.

“Over the last few years, the United States has moved into roughly $2 trillion deficits, even during peace and prosperity,” she added.

While deficits of three percent to four percent of GDP used to worry financial markets, she noted that levels are closer to six percent to seven percent of GDP now.

“That has made markets more nervous,” she said.

As inflation pushed interest rates higher, interest costs on the debt have risen as well, and costs linked to an ageing population are pushing up deficits.

– Risks ahead –

Analysts note that there is no debt-to-GDP level that automatically triggers a crisis.

Although the gross debt marks a symbolic threshold, many economists consider debt held by the public to be the most economically meaningful measure.

“But psychologically, these are the landmarks that warn financial markets that they need to take another look at rising debt,” Riedl said.

Federal borrowing surged during the Great Recession of 2007-2009 and increased following the government’s response to the downturn triggered by Covid-19, said Caleb Quakenbush, director of fiscal policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center.

But he told AFP that the trajectory of US budget spending has not been addressed by Congress or US administrations in a “meaningful or durable way.”

He warned of uncertainty surrounding the “unprecedented levels of borrowing that we’re seeing now.”

Bond markets could face steep challenges in a crisis scenario, he noted.

But even outside that situation, the United States could see higher borrowing costs for consumers and businesses, squeezing the economy.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had previously set a goal of cutting the US deficit to three percent of GDP.

articles.title: AI becomes the travel companion that talks people out of travelling
articles.description: Rather than encouraging people to visit more places
articles.summary: Rather than encouraging people to visit more places
articles.content:
For decades, travel planning has followed a familiar pattern. A traveller browses guidebooks, scans review sites, checks social media recommendations and builds an itinerary around the locations that seem most popular. Increasingly, however, another voice is entering the conversation: artificial intelligence. New research from AI platform MyIQ suggests that travellers are not simply using AI to discover new destinations. Instead, many are asking a different question: What is not worth my time?

The findings point to an emerging shift in travel behaviour, where artificial intelligence is acting as a filter between online popularity and real-world value. Rather than encouraging people to visit more places, AI is increasingly being used to identify attractions, experiences and destinations that may not live up to their reputation.

When popularity becomes a problem

The challenge for modern travellers is not a lack of information. It is the opposite. Travel advice can now be found almost everywhere, from specialist websites and influencer accounts to short-form videos and online forums. While this abundance of information offers unprecedented access to recommendations, it also creates uncertainty. Every attraction appears to be a “must-see”, every restaurant claims to be a hidden gem, and every social media post portrays an unforgettable experience.

As a consequence, many travellers are questioning whether highly promoted destinations genuinely merit the time and expense involved. According to the MyIQ survey, which collected responses from 5,934 adults across Canada, the U.S., U.K., Australia, Latin America and the European Union, 68% of respondents use AI when planning travel specifically to avoid disappointing experiences.

The research also found that 61% of those polled have asked AI whether a destination or attraction was actually worth visiting and 54% have used AI to identify places or experiences they suspected were overrated.

AI as a digital sceptic

One reason AI is proving useful is that many travellers perceive it as being less emotionally invested than social media creators or commercial travel websites. Influencers often depend on engagement, sponsorships and visual appeal. Tourism organisations seek to promote destinations. Travel companies are ultimately trying to sell experiences. In contrast, travellers increasingly view AI as an analytical tool capable of examining large numbers of reviews, ratings and opinions simultaneously.

Rather than asking, “Where should I go?”, users are asking questions such as “Is this attraction worth a three-hour queue?” and “Is this destination better than alternative options nearby?”

Artificial intelligence can aggregate and summarise large volumes of feedback far more rapidly than a human researcher could manage. The result is that AI functions less like a travel agent and more like a sceptical travelling companion, challenging assumptions before decisions are made.

articles.title: He Kept Getting Told Off for Doodling in Class. Then Nike Came Calling
articles.description: Joe Whale, better known as “The Doodle Boy,” turned the drawings that once got him in trouble at school into collaborations with some of the world’s biggest brands
articles.summary: Joe Whale, better known as “The Doodle Boy,” turned the drawings that once got him in trouble at school into collaborations with some of the world’s biggest brands
articles.content:
Getting told off in class for doodling probably does not sound like the beginning of a career. For Joe Whale, it was.

Whale, who is known online as “The Doodle Boy,” started drawing when he was very young. While attending school in Shrewsbury, England, he would finish his classwork quickly so he could spend the extra time drawing, but his teacher repeatedly told him to stop.

Instead of giving up on his drawings, his parents enrolled him in an after-school art class. His talent quickly became obvious. The instructor asked to see his sketchbook from home and was impressed enough to share one of his drawings on social media.

That post helped put Whale's work in front of a much larger audience.

His big breakthrough came after he was asked to create a doodle mural on the wall of a local restaurant. His father, Greg Whale, posted a video of him working on the mural, and the video reportedly received around 3 million views, bringing international attention to the young artist.

Offers began coming in.

By the time Whale was 12, he had signed a deal with Nike, becoming a co-creator for special projects. The partnership combined his artwork with Nike's focus on sport and creativity.

His father described the Nike partnership as a “dream come true” for Joe, who loved both sports and drawing.

articles.title: What Makes a Perfect Business in 2026? Three Mistakes Most Founders Still Make
articles.description: As artificial intelligence continues to reshape industries, many founders are rushing to automate everything they can
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence continues to reshape industries, many founders are rushing to automate everything they can
articles.content:
Yet according to entrepreneur Dan Bedford, most businesses are focusing on the wrong problem.

Dan Bedford, CEO of Connexion and Founder of Clio, believes that the strongest businesses in 2026 are not built around technology alone they are built around customer experience, sustainable value, and solving real-world problems.

Clio, a messaging platform that unifies WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook Messenger into a single automated workspace, was created to address a growing frustration among customers: ineffective AI-powered customer support.

The Customer Experience Problem

Businesses worldwide are investing billions into AI chatbots in pursuit of efficiency. However, Bedford argues that many companies prioritize their own operational convenience rather than the needs of their customers.

According to Bedford, most chatbot interactions feel impersonal and repetitive, often providing little more than automated versions of FAQ pages. As a result, many customers immediately request to speak with a human representative.

This disconnect between automation and genuine customer support has created an opportunity for businesses that can blend technology with meaningful communication.

Building From a Real Business Need

Unlike many startups that begin with a pitch deck, Clio was born from a practical challenge.

The inspiration came from Bedford's mother's education business in London, which offered government-funded training courses. While digital advertising generated thousands of leads, only a small percentage met the requirements for enrollment. Staff members spent significant time contacting unqualified prospects, creating unnecessary administrative costs.

To solve the issue, Bedford developed a WhatsApp-based workflow that automatically qualified leads, gathered required information, and pre-filled enrollment forms before a human representative became involved.

The results were significant:

  • 80% reduction in administrative costs
  • Faster lead qualification
  • Improved customer engagement
  • More productive sales teams

The project demonstrated a simple lesson: people prefer conversational interactions over lengthy forms, delayed emails, and complicated enrollment processes.

The AI Bubble Warning

While Bedford embraces artificial intelligence, he remains cautious about the current wave of AI-focused startups.

He compares today's AI investment surge to previous technology bubbles, warning founders against building businesses that rely entirely on third-party AI providers.

articles.title: Lisa Su: The CEO Powering AMD's AI Revolution
articles.description: Few technology leaders have transformed a company as dramatically as Lisa Su, the Chair and CEO of Advanced Micro Devices.
articles.summary: Few technology leaders have transformed a company as dramatically as Lisa Su, the Chair and CEO of Advanced Micro Devices.
articles.content:
Under her leadership, AMD has evolved from a struggling chipmaker into one of the world's most important semiconductor companies and a leading challenger in the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence market.

Today, AMD sits at the center of the global race to supply the processors powering AI models, cloud computing, supercomputers, and next-generation data centers.

The Turnaround That Changed AMD

When Lisa Su became AMD's CEO in 2014, the company faced significant challenges, including declining market share and financial difficulties.

Rather than competing on price alone, Su focused on long-term innovation, investing heavily in:

  • High-performance CPUs
  • Data-center processors
  • AI accelerators
  • Advanced chip architectures

The strategy transformed AMD into a major competitor in both consumer and enterprise computing.

A Key Player in the AI Boom

As artificial intelligence adoption accelerates worldwide, demand for powerful computing hardware has surged.

AMD has positioned itself as a major supplier of:

  • AI training processors
  • AI inference chips
  • Cloud computing infrastructure
  • High-performance data-center solutions

The company's latest AI accelerators are designed to help businesses run large language models and generative AI applications more efficiently.

With governments, enterprises, and technology companies investing billions in AI infrastructure, AMD has become one of the industry's biggest beneficiaries.

Competing in the Data Center Market

One of Lisa Su's biggest achievements has been AMD's growth in the data-center sector.

Its EPYC server processors have gained significant market share as cloud providers and enterprises seek alternatives for their computing needs.

articles.title: Sam Altman: The Visionary Driving the Artificial Intelligence Revolution
articles.description: As artificial intelligence transforms industries across the globe, Sam Altman has emerged as one of the most influential technology leaders of the modern era.
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence transforms industries across the globe, Sam Altman has emerged as one of the most influential technology leaders of the modern era.
articles.content:
As the Chief Executive Officer of OpenAI, Altman has played a central role in advancing generative AI, bringing powerful AI tools to businesses, researchers, and millions of everyday users worldwide.

Early Career


Born on April 22, 1985, in Chicago, Illinois, Sam Altman developed an interest in computers and programming from an early age. He attended Stanford University, where he studied computer science before leaving to pursue entrepreneurship.

His first startup, Loopt, was a location-based social networking company that participated in the prestigious Y Combinator startup accelerator. Although Loopt achieved moderate success, it marked the beginning of Altman's journey as a Silicon Valley entrepreneur.

Leading Y Combinator


In 2014, Altman became President of Y Combinator, one of the world's most successful startup accelerators. During his leadership, Y Combinator helped fund and mentor hundreds of startups, many of which became billion-dollar companies. His reputation as a visionary investor and entrepreneur grew rapidly throughout the technology industry.

Building OpenAI


Sam Altman became CEO of OpenAI in 2019, leading the organization through one of the fastest periods of innovation in artificial intelligence history.

Under his leadership, OpenAI introduced breakthrough technologies including:

  • ChatGPT
  • GPT-4 and GPT-5 language models
  • DALL·E image generation
  • Advanced AI tools for developers and enterprises

These technologies have transformed how people write, learn, create software, conduct research, and automate business operations.

AI for Everyone


Altman has consistently promoted the idea that artificial intelligence should benefit humanity while emphasizing the importance of responsible development and safety. OpenAI continues investing heavily in AI alignment, security, and research to ensure increasingly capable AI systems are deployed responsibly.

Industry Impact


Today, OpenAI is among the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, serving hundreds of millions of users and partnering with businesses across healthcare, finance, education, software development, and scientific research.

Altman is widely recognized as one of the key figures shaping the future of artificial intelligence and is frequently invited to speak with governments, policymakers, and global business leaders about AI's opportunities and challenges.

Looking Ahead


As AI becomes an increasingly important part of everyday life, Sam Altman's leadership continues to influence the direction of one of the most transformative technologies of the 21st century. His vision extends beyond today's AI assistants toward systems capable of solving complex scientific, medical, and economic challenges while expanding access to knowledge worldwide.

articles.title: Canada sets framework for responsible data centre development
articles.description: Create lasting local benefits for communities and Indigenous rights holders. For example, jobs and skills training
articles.summary: Create lasting local benefits for communities and Indigenous rights holders. For example, jobs and skills training
articles.content:
Canada’s data centre buildout now has a federal set of expectations to go alongside the provincial approaches.

The federal government released its Responsible Data Centre Development Principles, which set out five expectations for projects across the country. Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon announced the framework Thursday in Markham, Ont.

The principles say data centre projects must:

  • Create lasting local benefits for communities and Indigenous rights holders. For example, jobs and skills training.
  • Avoid shifting electricity costs to Canadians, and they can’t compromise grid reliability. When required, they need to contribute new supply, infrastructure, storage, or demand flexibility.
  • Minimize freshwater use and environmental impacts, with priority given to projects that are sustainable, with low-impact technologies and practices.
  • Disclose expected local impacts, engaging with impacted local and Indigenous communities early and transparently. Clear, independently verifiable information must be provided.
  • Bring what Ottawa calls “strategic value” to Canada.

Twenty-three companies have signed on, including Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Bell Canada, Cohere, Equinix, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, OVHcloud, Telus, and ThinkOn.

Ottawa says Canada relies significantly on infrastructure and services outside the country for the compute, cloud, and data storage that power AI. 

The federal release says more domestic capacity would give Canada greater resilience and choice while helping Canadian researchers, innovators, and businesses build and deploy AI.

The principles arrive after provinces started drawing their own lines around the same projects.

Ontario’s draft Data Centre Playbook proposes higher electricity rates for new data centres using more than one megawatt, along with requirements around local investment and keeping Canadian data in Canada. Saskatchewan went further last week and told new data centre developers to supply their own electricity. Alberta and B.C. have developed different approaches to grid access.

Ottawa says its principles are meant to “complement” provincial, territorial, municipal, and Indigenous regulatory processes. 

“These principles set a clear national standard,” says Solomon. “If you build in Canada, you must build responsibly and transparently and you must build for Canadians.”

Data centre approvals remain local decisions, and municipalities have good reason to want more information. 

A July Leger survey found 46% called AI data centre development in Canada a good thing and 37% called it a bad thing. Support narrowed when people were asked about projects in their own province, with 44% in favour and 42% opposed.

“No two data centre projects are alike, nor will they have the same impact. Municipal leaders need clear and complete information to make informed decisions,” says Tim Tierney, president of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, in a statement.

Ottawa has created a national framework of expectations. Provinces and municipalities still decide what gets built, where it goes, and what developers have to do before anyone turns on the power.

articles.title: Why real estate matters in modern investment portfolios today
articles.description: That decision is also being shaped by changes in allocation practice
articles.summary: That decision is also being shaped by changes in allocation practice
articles.content:
Institutional real estate remains a substantial market, yet size may not settle the allocation question. MSCI estimated that professionally managed global commercial property reached $13.5 trillion in 2025, an 8.5% increase influenced largely by currency movements. In separate research, MSCI reported that target allocations to real estate declined for the first time in 13 years. Scale alone may no longer secure a protected position.

The usual discussion centers on when transaction activity, valuations, and capital flows can recover. McKinsey reported that global real estate deal value rose approximately 12% to $873 billion in 2025, although transaction counts remained broadly flat. The figures suggest selective movement across the market. For institutional and individual investors, recovery may be only one part of a wider portfolio decision.

That decision is also being shaped by changes in allocation practice. Strategic asset allocation often assigns target weights to categories and periodically rebalances them. A total portfolio approach may begin with the objectives of the whole fund and assess each investment by its contribution to risk, return, and liquidity. CalPERS explains its approach in similarly holistic terms, evaluating investments within the context of the entire portfolio.

Competition across categories complicates the comparison. MSCI highlights that roughly 60% of investors view infrastructure and private credit as direct competitors to real estate. Its analysis also found substantial overlap in the distribution of individual real estate and infrastructure asset returns. The analysis directs attention toward underlying income, leverage, operating demands, and risks.

Geoffrey Dohrmann, chairman, CEO, and editor-in-chief of Institutional Real Estate, Inc. (IREI), views this as a structural change in how property must compete for capital. IREI is a media and market intelligence company serving institutional real estate and infrastructure markets through publications, data, research, events, and consulting. After decades observing allocators and managers, Dohrmann believes the next phase may require a clearer explanation of what each real estate strategy contributes across the portfolio.

Under fixed allocations, capital could flow to property partly because a fund needed to maintain its real estate target. Dohrmann observes that a total portfolio framework can place an office investment, a data center, an infrastructure asset, and a credit strategy into a more direct comparison. Real estate may still offer income, diversification, and exposure to physical demand, but managers may need to demonstrate those qualities through current evidence and appropriate pricing.

The category itself has already widened. Dohrmann recalls when institutional portfolios concentrated on office buildings, regional malls, warehouses, and a narrower definition of housing. “There isn’t any part of real estate that isn’t considered to be institutional class,” he explains, pointing to data centers, cold storage, medical offices, student housing, senior housing and marinas. The expansion may give allocators more ways to select assets around demographic and operational demand.

Selection is likely to carry greater weight within that broader field. MSCI researchers studied 1,086 portfolios and reported that asset selection accounted for an average of 67% of performance differences from country benchmarks between Q1 1999 and Q1 2025. Dohrmann explains a related lesson from IREI’s archives in simpler terms. He says, “The future arrives first as an unremarkable niche.” 

For managers, Dohrmann believes the change may reward sharper strategies, stronger operating capabilities and a more disciplined explanation of portfolio purpose. It may also encourage consolidation, platform extensions and recapitalizations when owners prefer to retain assets while bringing in replacement capital. Each route carries different risks. His broader point is that fundraising scale or category membership may provide limited reassurance unless the underlying assets can support the investment case.

Dohrmann also cautions against treating recent disappointment as a permanent verdict on property. Real estate continues to meet practical needs because people require places to live, work, store goods and receive services. He views its historical position between bonds and equities as useful context for thinking about income and growth. The appropriate role, however, may depend increasingly on the objectives and constraints of each portfolio.

Allocators can respond by defining that role before choosing a vehicle or manager. Dohrmann recommends asking which risk the investment is intended to offset, which cash flows support the expected return, and what evidence could weaken the thesis. Real estate can continue to attract institutional and individual investor capital. Its case can become more credible when every allocation begins with a clearly stated job and ends with evidence that the investment can perform it.

articles.title: YouTuber Chris Sails Faces Second Arrest Just Days After Alleged False Emergency
articles.description: Police say the claim triggered a major search involving boats, sonar equipment and drones before officers discovered the children were safe with family members.
articles.summary: Police say the claim triggered a major search involving boats, sonar equipment and drones before officers discovered the children were safe with family members.
articles.content:
A bizarre police call involving YouTuber Chris Sails quickly turned into a major emergency response, followed by two arrests in less than three days.

The incident began on August 16, 2026, when the Waller County Sheriff's Office in Texas responded to a report about a suspicious person allegedly running through a neighborhood and jumping onto residents' vehicles. According to court documents, an officer found Sails sitting in the roadway near a light pole and appearing to pray before he allegedly began rolling around in the street.

During the encounter, authorities said Sails told officers that his children had fallen into a body of water behind his home.

Police treated the claim as a real emergency and launched a search operation that involved fire department vehicles, rescue boats, specialized sonar equipment and aerial drones. The search was eventually stopped after authorities discovered that Sails' children were safe with family members and had not fallen into the water.

Sails was arrested on August 17 on a misdemeanor allegation of knowingly making a false statement to law enforcement. He was released the following day after posting bond.

The situation did not end there.

According to a second booking record, Sails was taken into custody again on August 20 at approximately 1:05 p.m., less than 69 hours after his first booking. The second arrest lists a charge of evading arrest or detention. Authorities have not publicly explained exactly what led to that second charge or whether it was directly connected to the original incident.

articles.title: UN Warns of Potentially Severe El Niño as Nations Prepare for Extreme Weather
articles.description: The United Nations has warned that the world could be entering a period of unusually severe weather as a powerful El Niño develops across the Pacific Ocean
articles.summary: The United Nations has warned that the world could be entering a period of unusually severe weather as a powerful El Niño develops across the Pacific Ocean
articles.content:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the planet was moving into a “danger zone of extreme weather” as the effects of the climate pattern begin to emerge in different parts of the world.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the current El Niño could become one of the strongest events recorded in more than seven decades and may continue until at least February 2027.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops when ocean temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific become significantly warmer than normal. The resulting changes in atmospheric circulation can alter weather patterns across large parts of the globe.

Some regions may face prolonged drought, while others could experience heavier rainfall, flooding, stronger storms and landslides. Higher temperatures are also expected in several areas, adding to the warming already being driven by climate change.

“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” Guterres warned, saying the combination of natural climate variability and long-term global warming could create particularly dangerous conditions.

Pacific Ocean Temperatures Rise Sharply

Scientists are closely monitoring rapidly increasing temperatures in the tropical Pacific.

Surface temperatures in the region used to monitor El Niño conditions have recently climbed more than 2°C above the average. Forecasts indicate that temperatures could approach 4°C above normal later this year.

If that occurs, the event could become the strongest El Niño since at least 1950.

Temperatures beneath the Pacific surface are even more unusual, with some areas measuring more than 8°C above average.

The warming is not limited to the Pacific. Above-average ocean temperatures are also expected in parts of the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around Australia.

Australia is particularly exposed because warmer seas can intensify marine heatwaves and put additional pressure on already vulnerable marine ecosystems.

Australia Prepares for Marine Threats

Australia has experienced severe marine heatwaves in recent years, contributing to coral bleaching, algae outbreaks and damage to marine ecosystems.

Scientists say El Niño can bring extreme heat that compounds these existing pressures.

The Great Barrier Reef may avoid the worst marine conditions this year, potentially giving damaged coral ecosystems additional time to recover. Southern Australia, however, faces greater concerns.

Previous marine heatwaves in South Australia and Tasmania have been associated with fish deaths, starving penguins, algae outbreaks and unusually large numbers of jellyfish.

Australia has introduced early-warning systems designed to provide authorities with more time to respond. These measures include preparing financial assistance for fisheries, relocating important species and increasing monitoring of coral reefs.
